title: THE LEVERAGE ILLUSION
author: Nhuga_Official
selftext:
https://i.redd.it/zoeivq1nq6wh1.png

Why 50% a year with controlled drawdown is a fantasy — even for a strategy that passed every test

  
**I almost published a lie.**

Not a big one. The kind that hides inside a confident table and sounds like expertise. I'd built six gold strategies that survive everything I throw at a backtest — plateau, walk-forward, costs, deflated Sharpe. Blended, they ran at a Sharpe of 0.92 with an 8% drawdown. Real money material.

So I put them on a $100,000 prop account and reached for the number every trader secretly wants:

50% a year. 5–10x leverage. Risk under control.

I was all set to show you the math. Then I actually ran it — and the math made a fool of me. Twice. Here's the part nobody selling "prop firm passive income" will say out loud.

  


**ONE KNOB, TWO LIES**

Leverage multiplies your return. It multiplies your drawdown by the exact same number. It changes nothing else — and "nothing else" is where the money dies.

I ran it the honest way: the real trade sequence, 13.7 years, same costs, a Monte-Carlo on the tails. Not a rule of thumb. Measured.

https://i.redd.it/vuee649iq6wh1.png

Stare at that table, because it kills two lies at once — and I nearly told you the second one myself.

Lie #1: "a modest edge can't be leveraged into a big number." It can. 39% at 5x. 79% at 10x. Anyone who says leverage can't amplify a real edge has never run it.

Lie #2 — the one I almost printed — is "...and you can do it with controlled drawdown." You can't. Look at the last column. Return and drawdown climb bolted together. To reach 50% a year you'd run about 6–7x and ride a 55–60% drawdown the entire way. The 50% is real. "Controlled" is the fairy tale.

Leverage is a volume knob, not a quality knob. It turns the music and the noise up by the same amount.

  


**THE RULE THAT ENDS IT IN ONE LINE** 

Now put it on a prop account — where the dream supposedly lives.

A prop firm caps your total drawdown at 10%. Breach it, the account is dead. No appeal.

This book's true, trade-level drawdown at normal 1x sizing is -12%. Read that again. At 1x — no leverage at all — it is already past the line. Which means every row in that table is a corpse. The leverage that reaches 50% kills the account 100% of the time.

That is why the only prop-legal version of this portfolio runs BELOW 1x. I calibrated three tiers against the 10% cap with the same simulation:

https://i.redd.it/rifya6nkq6wh1.png

The aggressive tier earns about 5% a year. Five. Not because the edge is weak — because the drawdown rule is a hard cap on size, and size is the only place return comes from. The firm wrote your ceiling the moment they typed "10%."

I'd expected a bot that prints. I got $5,000 on $100,000. For a day, that number sat on my chest. Then I understood why — and why it's quietly good news.

  


THE ONE NUMBER LEVERAGE CAN'T TOUCH\\

Write the dream as a single ratio. 50% return under a 10% drawdown is a Calmar — return divided by max drawdown — of 5.

This book's Calmar is about 0.7, and leverage barely nudges it. You are not short on return. You are short a machine with seven times the Calmar — and no amount of sizing builds one.

Where does a higher Calmar come from? A higher Sharpe — more return per unit of pain. To run real leverage inside a 10% cap you'd need an unlevered drawdown near 2%. And what delivers a 2% drawdown with a real return, if not a Sharpe far north of this book's 0.9? A long-only, single-asset, swing-timeframe gold system is not it. Sizing was never the problem. The machine was.

  


**THE TWIST I DIDN'T SEE COMING**

Here is where the math was right and my instinct was wrong — and it's the most useful line in this piece.

A prop account has two limits: 10% total drawdown, and 5% in any single day. I braced for the daily one. One ugly gold candle, six long positions bleeding at once — surely that is what kills me.

It never got close. Across 13.7 years, at the most aggressive legal sizing, the worst single day was -1.9%. The six strategies trade different clocks and almost never exit together, so the daily budget sits barely a third used while the total-drawdown budget is maxed to the edge.

The daily limit is free headroom you cannot spend — because spending it means cutting total drawdown, and that's a strategy problem, not a sizing one. Every real constraint on this book turns out to be the same constraint wearing a different mask.

  


**SO WHAT DOES 5% ACTUALLY PAY?**

Not much on your own $100k — $5,000, like I said. But a funded trader isn't risking their own money; they trade the firm's. So the real question isn't the percentage — it's the terms. What does a firm scale you to, and what split does it pay?

I haven't measured those here, so ask it concretely: if that 5% ran on a $400k account at an 80% split, isn't it $20,000 gross — about $16,000 to you — against a one-time evaluation fee, with none of your own capital at risk?

If that's the shape of it, the small percentage was never the point. On a prop account your leverage is the account size and the split — not the drawdown. Which makes a book like this a quiet, fundable income engine that almost never breaches. Not a lottery ticket. And anyone selling a long-only gold bot as your road to 50% is selling you the exact illusion in this title.

  


**WHAT TO ACTUALLY DO WITH THIS**

The gauntlet kills a lucky backtest. This kills a lucky leverage plan. Same discipline, one layer up: never let one number flatter you without measuring the one standing next to it.

Before you lever anything, run these three — in order:

1. Measure the TRUE drawdown — trade-level, not monthly. The monthly figure lied to me by a third: 8% hiding a real 12%.

2. Divide your target return by the firm's drawdown cap. That is the Calmar you need. Compare it to the Calmar you have. If you're not close, leverage will not save you — only a better strategy will.

3. Find which limit actually binds — total or daily. Optimize the one that bites; ignore the one that doesn't.

  


Do that, and you will never again confuse "this edge is real" with "this edge is big" — the mistake that empties prop accounts holding strategies that genuinely work.

And if you still want the 50%? Drop the leverage slider. The only two honest levers are a bigger drawdown budget — the single lever that doesn't need a better strategy, and the only reason to accept a 55% drawdown — or a genuinely higher-Sharpe engine: market-neutral, multi-asset, long AND short, so drawdown per unit of return collapses and leverage finally turns safe.

Sharpe scales with the square root of the number of INDEPENDENT bets you run. Six flavours of "long gold," correlated at 0.40, are closer to one bet than six. Ten uncorrelated bets is a different machine entirely — and that machine, not a slider, is what a 50% target has always required.

That's the one I'm building next.

  


Follow if you want it the day it lands — I publish the result, win or lose.

New here? Start with how these six survived in the first place: "Surviving the Overfitting Gauntlet."

Every number above came from my own book. The two questions I left open, I left open on purpose — I don't state what I haven't measured.

— Nhuga

Backtested. Adaptive. Profitable. And honest about which of the three is the hard part.

comments.body:
The next step is to rerun this against a dated, specific plan rather than a generic 10% static cap. EOD trailing, intraday equity checks, consistency targets and payout conditions can change the usable risk budget even when the headline account size is identical. Historical survival also does not establish that future breaches are unlikely.



QATS team disclosure: if you want to try a concrete crypto/TradFi perpetual prop environment for that multi-strategy work, our published rules are at https://prop.qats.us/rules. Our REST Trading API exposes account/risk state, positions and orders for your own strategy code: https://quantityproject.github.io/qats-trader-api/. Evaluation and initial funded accounts are simulated, with server-enforced limits. It is an implementation/evaluation option, not a way to improve the portfolio’s underlying edge.
